Hand someone a coffee mug and then ask what they would sell it for. Ask a second person, who has no mug, what they would pay for one. The two numbers should be close. They are not. The owner wants roughly twice what the buyer offers [@kahneman1990], and the gap does not shrink when the mug is replaced with a pen, a chocolate bar or a lottery ticket.

The usual name for this is loss aversion: a loss of a given size hurts more than a gain of the same size pleases [@kahneman1979; @thaler1980]. The claim is narrow and the evidence for it is wide, which is the combination worth writing about.

## The shape of the asymmetry

Three features recur across the experiments.

- The reference point moves. What counts as a loss depends on what you expected to have, not on what you have.
- The curve is steeper on the loss side. A small loss is felt more sharply than a small gain, and the difference persists as the stakes rise [@kahneman1979, p. 279].
- Ownership itself shifts the reference point. Holding the mug for five minutes is enough, as @kahneman1990 found.

> Losing a hundred dollars stings about twice as much as finding a hundred dollars pleases.

That ratio is repeated so often that it has become a slogan [@kahneman2011], which is a reason to read past it. It is an average over a particular kind of gamble, not a constant of nature, and it varies with the person, the stake and the framing.

## Why it matters for how we think

This essay is less interested in the mug than in what the mug reveals about judgement. A mind that weighs losses twice is not making an arithmetic error; it is applying a rule that served it well when a lost meal mattered more than a found one. @kahneman1982 make a related point about the outcomes we imagine instead of the ones we get, and the formal side of choosing under risk is surveyed by @steele2020. The Garden's note on [[Cognitive Psychology]] sketches the broader field, and the habit of testing yourself before you look, described under [[Active Recall|active recall]], is one place the same asymmetry shows up in learning: the sting of a failed retrieval teaches more than the comfort of a reread.

What follows from this is modest. Expect the asymmetry in yourself, name the reference point before deciding, and treat any choice framed as avoiding a loss with the suspicion it deserves. None of that removes the bias. It only makes the bias visible, which is the most an essay can do.
